egmo-2024-01.title: Obstructions, then build everything from -1
egmo-2024-01.body:
**Answer:** all pairs with $u\ne0$, $v\ne0$, $\max(u,v)>0$ and $\{u,v\}\ne\{-1,1\}$.

**These conditions are necessary.**
- If $u=0$ (or $v=0$), the board is $\{0,v\}$: operation 1 only gives $0+v=v$, which is already there, and operation 2 needs three numbers. Nothing new can ever be written.
- If $u,v<0$, all numbers stay negative: the sum of two negatives is negative, and for negative $a,b,c$ and $x\ge0$ we have $ax^2+bx+c\le c<0$, so operation 2 only produces negative roots.
- If $\{u,v\}=\{-1,1\}$, operation 1 adds only $0$. On the board $\{-1,0,1\}$ all sums of two different numbers are already present. For operation 2, $\{a,b,c\}=\{-1,0,1\}$ in some order. If $a=0$ the equation is $\pm x\pm1=0$, so $x=\pm1$. Otherwise the equation is one of $\pm(x^2-1)=0$ or $\pm(x^2-x)=0$, with roots in $\{-1,0,1\}$. So the board never grows beyond $\{-1,0,1\}$.

**These conditions are sufficient.** Let $u<v$ (so $v>0$), $u\ne0$, $\{u,v\}\ne\{-1,1\}$. Since $u,v\ne0$, the numbers $u,v,u+v$ are distinct; write $u+v$. The equation
$$ux^2+(u+v)x+v=(x+1)(ux+v)=0$$
has the root $x=-1$, so we can write $-1$ (if it is not there yet).

*Case $v=1$.* Then $u\le-2$. Adding $-1$ repeatedly to $u$ gives every integer below $u$. Adding $1$ repeatedly to $u$ gives $u+1,\dots,-1,0$ (each time the two summands differ). So every integer $\le1$ is on the board. Operation 2 with $(a,b,c)=(0,1,-2)$, i.e. $x-2=0$, gives $2$. Adding $1$ repeatedly then gives every integer $\ge2$.

*Case $v\ge2$.* Write $v+(-1)=v-1$, then $v+(v-1)=2v-1$, and in general $v+(kv-1)=(k+1)v-1$. This is allowed since $kv-1\ne v$ for $k\ge2$, $v\ge2$. So arbitrarily large numbers appear. From any positive number $a$ on the board we can add $-1$ repeatedly ($a\ne-1$) to get $a-1,a-2,\dots,0$. Hence every integer $\ge-1$ can be written. Then operation 2 with $(a,b,c)=(0,1,2)$, i.e. $x+2=0$, gives $-2$, and adding $-1$ repeatedly gives every integer $\le-3$.

So in both cases every integer can be written. ∎

egmo-2024-02.title: Show KT = KD, then the arc midpoint
egmo-2024-02.body:
**Step 1: $B,X,Y,C$ are concyclic.** Line $BC$ is tangent to the incircle at $D$, and $X$ lies on the arc on the other side of chord $DY$ from $C$. By the tangent–chord theorem, $\angle YDC=\angle DXY$. In triangle $DYC$, using $\angle CYD=\angle BXD$,
$$180^\circ=\angle DCY+\angle CYD+\angle YDC=\angle DCY+\angle BXD+\angle DXY=\angle BCY+\angle BXY,$$
since ray $XD$ lies inside $\angle BXY$ and $D$ lies on segment $BC$. So the opposite angles of quadrilateral $BXYC$ at $X$ and $C$ are supplementary, and $BXYC$ is cyclic.

**Step 2: $KT=KD$.** Using the power of $K$ with respect to $\Omega$, circle $BXYC$ and the incircle (tangent to line $BC$ at $D$):
$$KT^2=KB\cdot KC=KX\cdot KY=KD^2 .$$

**Step 3: $TD$ passes through the midpoint $M$ of arc $BC$ not containing $A$.** Let line $TD$ meet $\Omega$ again at $M'$ ($D$ is inside $\Omega$, so $M'\ne T$, and $D$ lies between $T$ and $M'$). Let $t$ be the tangent to $\Omega$ at $M'$. We use directed angles between lines.
- The reflection in the perpendicular bisector of $TM'$ swaps $T$ and $M'$, maps the tangent $KT$ at $T$ to the tangent $t$ at $M'$, and fixes line $TM'$. Reflections reverse directed angles, so $\measuredangle(t,TM')=-\measuredangle(KT,TM')$.
- Since $KT=KD$, the reflection in the perpendicular bisector of $TD$ (through $K$) swaps lines $KT$ and $KD$ and fixes line $TD=TM'$. So $\measuredangle(KD,TM')=-\measuredangle(KT,TM')$.

Hence $\measuredangle(t,TM')=\measuredangle(KD,TM')$, i.e. $t\parallel KD=BC$. The only points of $\Omega$ whose tangent is parallel to $BC$ are the two midpoints of the arcs $BC$. Since $D\in BC$ lies between $T$ and $M'$ and $T$ is on the same side of $BC$ as $A$, the point $M'$ is on the opposite side. So $M'=M$, the midpoint of arc $BC$ not containing $A$.

The bisector $AI$ of $\angle BAC$ passes through $M$. So lines $TD$ and $AI$ meet at $M\in\Omega$. ∎

egmo-2024-03.title: Classify the peculiar numbers
egmo-2024-03.body:
**Step 1: at most two prime factors.** Let $n>1$ be peculiar and $d>1$ a divisor of $n$. Applying the definition to the divisor $n/d$:
$$\frac nd\left(\frac nd+1\right)\ \Big|\ n(n+1)\iff n(n+d)\mid d^2n(n+1)\iff n+d\mid d^2(n+1).$$
Since $n\equiv-d\pmod{n+d}$, we get $d^2(n+1)\equiv d^2(1-d)$, so $n+d\mid d^3-d^2$, which is positive. Hence $n+d\le d^3-d^2$ and $n<d^3$. Take $d=p$, the smallest prime factor of $n$. All prime factors of $n$ are $\ge p$, so $n$ has at most two prime factors counted with multiplicity: $n=p$, $n=p^2$ or $n=pq$ with distinct primes.

**Step 2: $n=p^2$ is impossible.** The divisor $p$ gives $p(p+1)\mid p^2(p^2+1)$, so $p+1\mid p(p^2+1)$. Since $\gcd(p+1,p)=1$, $p+1\mid p^2+1=(p+1)(p-1)+2$, so $p+1\mid2$. Impossible.

**Step 3: $n=pq$ forces $p=q^2-q-1$.** Let $p>q$ be primes and $n=pq$ peculiar. The divisor $p$ gives $p+1\mid q(pq+1)$. As $pq+1=q(p+1)-(q-1)$, this means $p+1\mid q(q-1)$. Symmetrically the divisor $q$ gives $q+1\mid p(p-1)$.
- If $q\nmid p+1$, then $\gcd(p+1,q)=1$ and $p+1\mid q-1$, impossible as $0<q-1<p+1$. So $p+1=mq$ for some integer $m\ge1$, and $mq\mid q(q-1)$ gives $m\mid q-1$, so $m\le q-1$.
- $p\nmid q+1$: otherwise $p=q+1$, so $(p,q)=(3,2)$, but then $p+1=4\nmid q(q-1)=2$. Hence $q+1\mid p-1=mq-2=m(q+1)-(m+2)$, so $q+1\mid m+2$ and $m\ge q-1$.

Therefore $m=q-1$ and $p=q(q-1)-1=q^2-q-1$.

**Conclusion.** Every peculiar number is $1$, a prime, or $pq$ with primes $q<p=q^2-q-1$. Suppose a prime $r$ divides four different peculiar numbers. Each is $r$ itself or of the form $pq$ with $r\in\{p,q\}$:
- if $r=q$ is the smaller prime, the number is $r(r^2-r-1)$;
- if $r=p$ is the larger one, then $r=q^2-q-1$, and $q$ is determined by $r$ because $q\mapsto q^2-q-1$ is increasing.

So at most three peculiar numbers are divisible by $r$, a contradiction. Hence no prime divides all of $A,B,C,D$, and $\gcd(A,B,C,D)=1$. ∎

*(Three can share a factor, e.g. $5$, $15=3\cdot5$ and $95=5\cdot19$.)*

egmo-2024-04.title: Powers of two and the half-length bound
egmo-2024-04.body:
**Answer:** $\dfrac{(n-1)(n-2)}2+1$.

**Construction.** Let $a_1=0$ and $a_i=2^i$ for $2\le i\le n$.
- For $2\le j\le n-1$: $\frac{a_{j+1}-a_1}{a_j-a_1}=\frac{2^{j+1}}{2^j}=2$, so $(a_1,a_j)$ is interesting.
- For $2\le i<j\le n-1$: $\frac{a_{j+1}-a_{i+1}}{a_j-a_i}=\frac{2^{j+1}-2^{i+1}}{2^j-2^i}=2$.
- $(a_{n-1},a_n)$: $a_n-a_{n-1}=2^{n-1}$ and $a_n-a_1=2^n$.

So all $\binom{n-1}2$ pairs with $j\le n-1$, and also $(a_{n-1},a_n)$, are interesting: $\binom{n-1}2+1$ pairs.

**Upper bound.** There are $\binom n2$ pairs, and $\binom n2-\left(\binom{n-1}2+1\right)=n-2$, so we must find $n-2$ pairs that are not interesting. Let $L=a_n-a_1$, the largest difference.
- If $(a_i,a_j)$ is interesting, then $2(a_j-a_i)=a_\ell-a_k\le L$, so $a_j-a_i\le\frac L2$. In particular $(a_1,a_n)$ is not interesting.
- For $2\le i\le n-1$: $(a_i-a_1)+(a_n-a_i)=L$. If both $(a_1,a_i)$ and $(a_i,a_n)$ were interesting, both differences would be $\le\frac L2$, hence both $=\frac L2$, i.e. $a_i=\frac{a_1+a_n}2$. This holds for at most one $i$.

So for at least $n-3$ indices $i\in\{2,\dots,n-1\}$, one of $(a_1,a_i)$, $(a_i,a_n)$ is not interesting. These pairs are distinct for distinct $i$, and different from $(a_1,a_n)$. Together with $(a_1,a_n)$ we get at least $n-2$ pairs that are not interesting. Hence at most $\binom{n-1}2+1$ pairs are interesting. ∎

egmo-2024-05.title: Everything is a power of one prime
egmo-2024-05.body:
Let $\tau(n)$ be the number of positive divisors of $n$.

**Answer:** $f(n)=q^{\tau(n)-1}$ for a fixed prime $q$.

**These work.** Clearly $\tau(f(n))=\tau(n)$. If $x\nmid y$ and $y\nmid x$, then $g=\gcd(x,y)$ is a proper divisor of both $x$ and $y$. Every divisor of $g$ divides $x$, and $x$ itself does not divide $g$, so $\tau(g)<\tau(x)$; similarly $\tau(g)<\tau(y)$. Hence
$$\gcd(f(x),f(y))=q^{\min(\tau(x),\tau(y))-1}\ge q^{\tau(g)}>q^{\tau(g)-1}=f(g).$$

**Nothing else works.** Let $f$ satisfy the conditions. The key tool: *if $q^e\mid M$ and $M$ has a prime factor other than $q$, then $\tau(M)\ge2(e+1)$.*
- $f(1)=1$ (the only number with one divisor), and $f(p)$ is a prime for every prime $p$. For a prime $p\ne2$, condition 2 for $(2,p)$ gives $\gcd(f(2),f(p))>f(1)=1$, so $f(p)=f(2)$. Let $q=f(2)$; then $f(p)=q$ for all primes $p$.
- It suffices to show that **every $f(n)$ is a power of $q$**: then $\tau(f(n))=\tau(n)$ forces $f(n)=q^{\tau(n)-1}$.

*Prime powers: $f(p^t)=q^t$.* Induction on $t$; $t=0,1$ are done. Assume it for all exponents $\le m$, where $m\ge1$, and let $r\ne p$ be a prime.
- The pair $(p^{m-1}r,\,p^m)$ satisfies the hypothesis of condition 2, and the gcd is $p^{m-1}$. So $\gcd(f(p^{m-1}r),q^m)>q^{m-1}$, i.e. $q^m\mid f(p^{m-1}r)$. This number has $\tau(p^{m-1}r)=2m<2(m+1)$ divisors, so by the key tool it is a power of $q$, namely $q^{2m-1}$.
- The pair $(p^{m+1},\,p^{m-1}r)$, with gcd $p^{m-1}$, gives $\gcd(f(p^{m+1}),q^{2m-1})>q^{m-1}$, so $q^m\mid f(p^{m+1})$. Since $\tau(f(p^{m+1}))=m+2<2(m+1)$, $f(p^{m+1})$ is a power of $q$, so it equals $q^{m+1}$.

*General $n$.* Induction on the number $k\ge1$ of distinct prime factors; $k=1$ is done. Assume $f$ is a power of $q$ on all numbers with at most $k$ distinct prime factors. Fix a prime $p$. We show by induction on $m\ge0$: for every $N$ with exactly $k$ distinct prime factors and $p\nmid N$, $f(Np^m)$ is a power of $q$. For $m=0$ this is the hypothesis. Suppose it holds for $m$, and let $s$ be a prime factor of $N$.
- The pair $(Np^{m+1},\,Nsp^m)$: neither divides the other (compare the exponents of $p$ and of $s$), and the gcd is $Np^m$.
- $f(Np^m)=q^{\tau(Np^m)-1}$. Also $f(Nsp^m)=f\big((Ns)p^m\big)$ is a power of $q$ by the inductive hypothesis for $m$, as $Ns$ has $k$ distinct prime factors. So condition 2 gives $q^{\tau(Np^m)}\mid f(Np^{m+1})$.
- $\tau(f(Np^{m+1}))=(m+2)\tau(N)<2\big((m+1)\tau(N)+1\big)$, so by the key tool $f(Np^{m+1})$ is a power of $q$.

Every number with $k+1$ distinct prime factors has the form $Np^m$ ($m\ge1$) as above, which completes the induction. Hence $f(n)=q^{\tau(n)-1}$. ∎

egmo-2024-06.title: Examples for d ≤ 3, root-neighbour counting for d ≥ 4
egmo-2024-06.body:
**Answer: $d=1,2,3$.**

**Examples.**
- $d=1$: $P(x)=x$; there is a single value $P(0)$.
- $d=2$: $P(x)=x(x-1)$; the values at $0,1,2$ are $0,0,2$.
- $d=3$: $P(x)=x(x-4)(x-5)$; the values at $0,1,\dots,6$ are $0,12,12,6,0,0,12$.

**No example for $d\ge4$.** Suppose $P$ works, let $N=d^2-d$, let $V$ be the set of values $P(0),\dots,P(N)$, and for $v\in V$ let $n_v$ be the number of $m\in\{0,\dots,N\}$ with $P(m)=v$. Since $P-v$ has at most $d$ roots, $n_v\le d$. As $\sum n_v=N+1=d^2-d+1>d(d-1)$, we need $|V|=d$. Write $V=\{p_1<\dots<p_d\}$ and $n_i=n_{p_i}$.

**Claim 1.** If $n_i=d$ and $j=i\pm1\in\{1,\dots,d\}$, then $n_j\le d-2$.

*Proof.* Let $r_1<\dots<r_d$ be the positions of $p_i$, so $P(x)-p_i=c\prod_k(x-r_k)$. Let $\varepsilon=\operatorname{sign}(p_j-p_i)$ and $g=\varepsilon(P-p_i)$. By Rolle, $P'$ has a root in each $(r_k,r_{k+1})$; these are all $d-1$ roots of $P'$. So $g$ is strictly monotone on $I_0=(-\infty,r_1)$ and on $I_d=(r_d,\infty)$, and on each $I_k=(r_k,r_{k+1})$ it has exactly one turning point; so on a positive $I_k$ it strictly rises and then strictly falls. The signs of $g$ on $I_0,\dots,I_d$ alternate; call an interval *positive* if $g>0$ on it. Let $S$ be the set of positions of $p_j$. Key fact: if $u\in\{0,\dots,N\}$ and $g(u)>0$, then $g(u)\ge|p_j-p_i|$, because $P(u)\in V$ is on the same side of $p_i$ as $p_j$, and $p_j$ is the value of $V$ nearest to $p_i$ on that side.

*(a) Where $S$ can lie.* Each $m\in S$ has $g(m)=|p_j-p_i|>0$, so $m$ lies in a positive interval.
- If $m\in I_k$ with $1\le k\le d-1$ and $r_k+1<m<r_{k+1}-1$, then $g(m)>\min\big(g(r_k+1),g(r_{k+1}-1)\big)\ge|p_j-p_i|$. Impossible, so $m\in\{r_k+1,r_{k+1}-1\}$.
- If $m\in I_d$ and $m>r_d+1$, then $g(m)>g(r_d+1)\ge|p_j-p_i|$ (here $r_d+1<m\le N$). So $m=r_d+1$. Similarly $m\in I_0$ forces $m=r_1-1$.

So $S$ is contained in the list $L$ whose *entries* are $r_k+1$ and $r_{k+1}-1$ for every positive inner $I_k$, plus $r_d+1$ if $I_d$ is positive and $r_1-1$ if $I_0$ is positive. Counting positive intervals in the alternating pattern shows $L$ has exactly $d$ entries.

*(b) Right end.* Note $|P(x)-p_i|=|c|\prod_k|x-r_k|$.
- If $I_d$ is positive (then so is $I_{d-2}$), consider the entries $r_d+1$ and $r_{d-1}-1$:
$$\frac{|P(r_d+1)-p_i|}{|P(r_{d-1}-1)-p_i|}=\frac{(r_d+1-r_{d-1})\prod_{k\le d-2}(r_d+1-r_k)}{(r_d-r_{d-1}+1)\prod_{k\le d-2}(r_{d-1}-1-r_k)}>1,$$
since $0<r_{d-1}-1-r_k<r_d+1-r_k$ for $k\le d-2$. (If $r_{d-1}-1=r_{d-2}$, then $r_{d-1}-1$ is a root of $P-p_i$ and is not in $S$ anyway.)
- If $I_{d-1}$ is positive, consider $r_{d-1}+1$ and $r_d-1$. When these are different points (so $r_{d-1}+1<r_d-1$),
$$\frac{|P(r_d-1)-p_i|}{|P(r_{d-1}+1)-p_i|}=\frac{1\cdot(r_d-1-r_{d-1})\prod_{k\le d-2}(r_d-1-r_k)}{(r_d-r_{d-1}-1)\cdot1\cdot\prod_{k\le d-2}(r_{d-1}+1-r_k)}>1,$$
since $r_d-1-r_k>r_{d-1}+1-r_k>0$ for $k\le d-2$.

Points of $S$ all have $|P-p_i|=|p_j-p_i|$, so **at most one point of this right pair is in $S$**.

*(c) Left end.* $|P(x)-p_i|$ depends only on the distances to the $r_k$, so the mirror-image argument shows that **at most one point of the left pair** ($r_1-1$ and $r_2+1$ if $I_0$ is positive, or $r_1+1$ and $r_2-1$ if $I_1$ is positive) is in $S$.

*(d)* For $d\ge4$ the two pairs are four different entries of $L$: they come from $I_d,I_{d-2}$ or $I_{d-1}$ on the right and from $I_0,I_2$ or $I_1$ on the left. The only coincidence of intervals is $I_{d-2}=I_2$ when $d=4$, and then the right pair uses its right entry and the left pair its left entry. Hence
$$|S|\le(d-4)+1+1=d-2.\qquad\square$$

**Counting.** By Claim 1, $n_i+n_{i+1}\le2d-2$ for every $1\le i\le d-1$: if one of them is $d$ the other is $\le d-2$, and otherwise both are $\le d-1$.
- *$d$ even:* $d^2-d+1=\sum n_i=(n_1+n_2)+\dots+(n_{d-1}+n_d)\le\frac d2(2d-2)=d^2-d$. Contradiction.
- *$d\ge5$ odd:* $d^2-d+1=n_1+(n_2+n_3)+\dots+(n_{d-1}+n_d)\le d+\frac{d-1}2(2d-2)=d^2-d+1$. So equality holds: $n_1=d$ and every pair $(n_i,n_{i+1})$ sums to $2d-2$. Then Claim 1 gives $n_2=d-2$, hence $n_3=d$, and so on: $n_i=d$ for odd $i$ and $n_i=d-2$ for even $i$.

**The odd case.** Replacing $P$ by $-P$ reverses the order of $V$ and keeps this pattern ($d+1-i\equiv i\pmod2$), so we may assume the leading coefficient $c>0$. Fix an odd $i\le d-2$ and take $j=i+1$, so $\varepsilon=+1$. Since $d$ is odd and $c>0$, $I_d$ is positive and $I_0$ negative, so the right pair is $\{r_{d-1}-1,r_d+1\}$ and the left pair lies in $I_1$. Since $|S|=n_{i+1}=d-2$, all bounds in (d) are tight: every entry of $L$ outside the two pairs is a point of $S$, and exactly one point of each pair is in $S$.
- *$r_d+1\notin S$.* Otherwise, by (b), $0\le P(r_{d-1}-1)-p_i<p_{i+1}-p_i$. Since $P(r_{d-1}-1)\in V$, this forces $P(r_{d-1}-1)=p_i$, i.e. $r_{d-1}-1=r_{d-2}$. But then the entry $r_{d-2}+1=r_{d-1}$ of $I_{d-2}$ lies outside both pairs, so it is in $S$, whereas $P(r_{d-1})=p_i$. Contradiction. So $r_{d-1}-1\in S$.
- Hence both entries of $I_3$ are in $S$ (for $d=5$, $I_3=I_{d-2}$ and its right entry $r_4-1$ was just shown to be in $S$): $P(r_3+1)=P(r_4-1)=p_{i+1}$, where $r_3<r_4$ are the 3rd and 4th positions of $p_i$.

*Monotone blocks.* $P-p_1$ has $d$ distinct roots, so $P'$ has $d-1$ distinct simple roots $e_1<\dots<e_{d-1}$. Let $B_t$ be the set of integers of $[0,N]$ in $[e_{t-1},e_t)$ (with $e_0=-\infty$, $e_d=+\infty$). $P$ is strictly monotone on each $[e_{t-1},e_t]$: increasing for odd $t$ and decreasing for even $t$ (as $c>0$ and $d$ is odd). So a value occurs at most once in each block. For odd $i$, $n_i=d$ forces $p_i$ to occur exactly once in every block, and its $t$-th position is in $B_t$.

Now look at $B_3$ (increasing). For odd $i\le d-2$, $p_i$ occurs in $B_3$ at $r_3$. Since $p_d>p_i$ occurs later in $B_3$, the point $r_3+1$ also lies in $B_3$, and it carries $p_{i+1}$. So $B_3$ contains all odd and all even values: it is $d$ consecutive integers $u,\dots,u+d-1$ with $P(u+k)=p_{k+1}$. In the same way $B_4$ (decreasing; $p_d$ occurs before $r_4$, so $r_4-1\in B_4$) is $w-d+1,\dots,w$ with $P(w-k)=p_{k+1}$.

Let $Q(x)=P(x)-P(u+w-x)$. As $d$ is odd, its leading coefficient is $2c\ne0$, so $\deg Q=d$. But $Q(u+k)=0$ and $Q(w-k)=0$ for $k=0,\dots,d-1$, which gives $2d$ distinct roots ($B_3$ and $B_4$ are disjoint). Contradiction.

So no polynomial works for $d\ge4$, and the answer is $d\in\{1,2,3\}$. ∎
